    #20706. Breaking: WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2691 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that wordPress 7.2 is due on Dec.
    • Switching it off will require coding, as there are no settings available via the WordPress dashboard to disable this feature.
    • That makes /random/ the 7.2 change most sites will need to decide on before updating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that wordPress 7.2 is due on Dec. 8. This version has, in beta, turned on a new public address on updated sites. /random/ directs you to a random published post. Versions of the address also do this within categories, tags, author archives, or eligible custom post types.

    This feature is on by default. Switching it off will require coding, as there are no settings available via the WordPress dashboard to disable this feature. Further, in the November roundup of the WordPress Developer Blog, the filter name listed doesn’t match the actual filter name used in the code. Copying the name from the Developer Blog will have no effect.

    That makes /random/ the 7.2 change most sites will need to decide on before updating. The upcoming Secrets API, a way for plugins to store credentials, was removed from 7.2 on Nov. 17. That came days after Matt Mullenweg, who leads the release, sided with a request to pull it.

    Core’s new AI pieces are tools for developers and plugins, and none of them adds an AI feature visitors or editors will see.

    Sources indicate that beta five is the latest test release, and WordPress states not to run it on production sites. The first release candidate (RC1) is due Nov. 17, so details can still change before the final release.

    In a recent development, aaron Jorbin’s developer note opens, “A request to example.com/random/ will lead end owners to a randomly selected published post. The feature is on by default.”.

    The /random/ path and its category, tag, author, and post type versions use the default base with pretty permalinks. The base is translatable, and a new field on the Permalinks screen changes it. The development code also responds to a random query variable, so ?random works too on the home page and archives. Since a Nov. 16 change, a search URL that includes it redirects to the same search without the parameter.

    Recent findings suggest that by default, posts are eligible. Pages and attachments aren’t. Custom post types are considered eligible if they’re publicly queryable, have archives and the developer hasn’t registered them with 'randomable' => false. The code filters for only published posts (with no password).

    According to recent reports, it uses a 302 redirect. The development code sends no-cache headers and includes the header X-Robots-Tag: noindex, follow with the 302 redirect response. This header covers the original /random/ request, but not the post this redirects to. If there is no match to the query, the request will return a 404.

    In a recent development, if you’ve created a published page with the slug “random,” then this will override the redirect. The same thing happens if you create a post with the slug “random,” when permalinks are set to use the post name. Peter Wilson confirmed this in the comments after Daniel Iser raised it, and recommended using a base like “shuffle” instead.

    Recent findings suggest that random queries run from the main WP_Query, so pre_get_posts callbacks that change archives will also affect their random redirect. Developers wishing to target random requests only should use wp_is_random_content_query().

    Industry observers note that turning this feature off is done by adding the one-line mu-plugin shown in the note, add_filter( 'wp_enable_random_content_redirect', '__return_false' );. This will prevent WordPress from generating rewrite rules for random content, hide the base field on the Permalinks screen, and ignore the query variable. The code’s documentation indicates that flushing the rewrite rules is necessary after changing the filter value.

    The roundup’s version, wp_enable_random_content_direct, isn’t used anywhere in the code.

    Recent findings suggest that random redirects made their initial appearance in the code on Sept. 21; at this point they were an optional ?random query that needed sites to return true for a filter called enable_random_content_redirect if they wanted them to be active.

    They were reverted two days after that. The commit message mentioned of the feature, “The feature is intended to land in WordPress 7.2 but will need some work.”.

    Sources indicate that on Oct. 16, they returned as /random/ rewrite rules turned on, with the filter name changed and the default for the filter set to true. They were added to Beta 1 on Oct. 20.

    Jorbin’s post drew a long thread of objections. Joost de Valk wrote, “This is a horrible idea to turn on by default.” In a later reply, he added, “Now I fear people will randomly end up on invoices, offers, client specific pages, etc.” Responding to another commenter, Jorbin wrote, “The WordPress Philosophies mean that opt-out options are not added for every feature, otherwise the options pages would become unusable.”.

    Mullenweg replied to a commenter whose site already has a page named “random,” writing, “I agree it should not use page URL structure.” In a separate comment, he wrote, “I don’t think this should be an appended pretty URL; the request was just for /?random, just at root.” He also addressed concerns about performance and exposure, saying query strings, searches, and REST calls offer “far more ways” to exhaust a site’s resources.

    Industry observers note that as of Nov. 17, no one maintaining the feature had posted a change to its default or its URL structure. Since the note, code changes from Nov. 12 to Nov. 17 have adjusted when the redirect fires, how it treats searches and how it picks a post.

    See also: Web Almanac Data Reveals CMS Plugins Are Setting Technical SEO Standards (Not SEOs).

    The Secrets API would have allowed plugins to save API keys, tokens and more via libsodium encryption, and would have utilized the options tables, which hosts could replace with their own keyring or storage utilizing a secrets.php drop-in.

    Recent findings suggest that wordPress reverted the API on Nov. 17. The commit points to feedback on the announcement that questioned the design, including whether one API should both write secrets and read the ones a host supplies. Peter Wilson had also found that the API never checked its manage_secrets and manage_network_secrets capabilities when secrets were set. The commit message opens, “Removes the Secrets API from WordPress 7.2 to allow more time for the API to mature before it ships in a future release.”.

    Industry observers note that earlier, Ryan McCue, a contributor, had commented that he believes secrets managed outside WordPress should only be readable and never writable to WordPress and that allowing writes to be part of this feature and easy to accomplish makes the API “likely to ossify” around that design. He argued that, under this design, a secrets store backed by hardware security modules offered no additional protection over an already encrypted database. He concluded, “I am a strong -1 on this feature, and I think this should be backed out of core for 7.2 until the above is resolved.”.

    Mullenweg replied, “I agree with @rmccue here.” Two minutes later, he wrote, “It’s also not a great time to be making ourselves a target for very sensitive things like that.”.

    Eric Mann, the writer of the developer note, responded to the encryption point, writing, “Encryption at rest protects against someone walking off with the disk. It does nothing about SQL injection, a leaked mysqldump, a misconfigured backup bucket.” Mann initially wanted to leave the API in 7.2 and referenced a proposed solution for how the AI plugin handles failed write operations, one of the items that was mentioned by McCue.

    After Wilson’s finding, Mann replied, “I’m not excited about it but agree more time will help us ship a more solid foundation here. I’d still like to target at least 7.3 if possible.”.

    The AI plugin version 1.5.0 (released Oct. 29) moved its opt-in Key Encryption experiment into a bundled version of the Secrets API which stores the plugin’s AI service keys. Its maintainers had a pull request open to revision it to the version planned for core. After the revert, Jeffrey Paul, who had approved it, wrote that the plugin should “use an approach here that leverages the functionality outside of core” instead. The pull request was still open on Nov. 17, and 1.5.0 was still the latest release.

    See also: When The WordPress Plugin Enhancement Is The Security Risk: Why SEOs Should Pay Attention.

    WordPress put AI building blocks into core before this release. Roger Montti reported in May that 7.0 shipped four of them, including the WP AI Client and a Connectors screen for AI services. In October, he reported that WordPress had released a canonical MCP Adapter plugin for connecting AI systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

    Sources indicate that wordPress 7.2 is set to add three newly introduced read-only abilities, which are registered actions called by other applications. The new read-only abilities allow other applications to query content, owners, and WordPress settings. A developer will be able to build an embedding, a numeric representation of text, through the AI client to provide similarity search functionality.

    Sources indicate that in addition to adding the three read-only abilities, the WordPress core team has marked those abilities as exposed to clients such as the WordPress core REST API, MCP, or AI agents. According to the documentation, “Exposure flags do not grant execution permission.” The content query ability requires a logged-in user and checks if the user has read permission for the returned posts. There is right now no MCP server included in the WordPress core.

    According to a post released about version 1.5.0 of the AI plugin, the AI plugin provides versions of these newly introduced abilities that are expected to be identical to the versions “coming in WordPress core with 7.2 this December.” Additionally, the post notes there are breaking changes in how existing integrations work because of this patch.

    In a recent development, the AI features editors will experience live within the AI plugin itself, where they are currently being tested as opt-in experiments with different requirements; two examples include text-to-speech and revision summaries where content is sent to the site’s selected AI provider. In addition, Content Verification identifies C2PA Content Credentials, a standard for providing provenance information for digital media. However, according to the release post, Content Verification “does not yet perform cryptographic verification” of C2PA Content Credentials. Another feature, MCP Access, decides what the plugin makes available over MCP.

    The AI plugin’s screenshot reveals the “Unverified” notice displayed when Content Credentials are detected.

    The AI plugin flags detected Content Credentials as unverified. Screenshot: WordPress AI.

    Supporting broader types of agents in the future is part of plans for the next release. WordPress’s agentic-web proposal says, “Agents can already accomplish a lot with WordPress through WP-CLI, the REST API, and file management. However, these approaches often require local access or more advanced configurations.” The agentic-web proposal plans to implement support for WordPress 7.3 and is planning to develop foundational elements during the 7.2 cycle.

    Industry observers note that admin and login screens in 7.2 separate the combined JavaScript and style sheets they once had into individual assets. According to the roundup, this means each asset is loaded separately by WordPress, which has also included prefetching of the assets needed for the next screen it thinks you’ll be viewing. load-scripts.php and load-styles.php have been deprecated in this version. This change applies to the admin and login screens only.

    Industry observers note that the fresh SVG icons in the admin bar and menu replace the ones previously made available via the Dashicons font. So if your plugins used CSS to add additional styling to those icons’ ::before content, you may want to review them. Beta 5 introduced notification emails when an application password was created. Also according to WordPress, 7.2 aims to include full support for PHP 8.6.

    The preview below demonstrates the fresh icons in the WordPress admin menu.

    Sources indicate that new icons in the WordPress 7.2 admin menu. Screenshot: WordPress Developer Blog.

    Recent findings suggest that whether to keep /random/ active is probably the decision most WordPress sites will have to make by Dec. 8. Unless /random/ is turned off, all published posts without a password (including content from a custom post type that is publicly queryable with an archive) can randomly appear. Some commenters on Jorbin’s post thought that would be true for some testimonial or client page custom post types they had created, even though those are not included in the site’s navigation links. First, check which of your custom post types are publicly queryable and have an archive. Then, for any of those custom post types that shouldn’t appear, set 'randomable' => false so that they won’t show up through this method.

    In a recent development, the noindex header isn’t applied to the posts /random/ points to, and the selection made by WordPress doesn’t automatically skip posts an SEO plugin has set to noindex. There was still no response as of Nov. 16 to a commenter who questioned that in the developer notes. Consumers of SEO plugins that prevent access to posts via search engines may want to determine if /random/ will still be able to reach those posts.

    In a recent development, on sites behind a page cache or CDN, /random/ can return a 404 right after the upgrade. According to the hosting team, that lasts until rewrite rules are flushed, which core does on the first wp-admin request after the upgrade, per site on multisite. On the platform the team tested, a cached 404 stayed after the upgrade until the cache was purged. One tester using shared hosting without a page cache found the rules already in place. To help prevent a stale 404 from being served, purge the page cache after the first admin visit.

    McCue raised the load that the selection’s random ordering could put on large sites, especially if bots hit /random/ repeatedly. Jorbin stated on Nov. 10 that he had opened a ticket to look at performance on very large sites, and a fix landed on Nov. 17. It looks up random post IDs instead of sorting the archive at random, a method the commit says “keeps the cost of a request independent of the number of posts”. Archives whose posts are too sparse among the post IDs fall back to a cached pool of up to 1,000 randomly ordered posts. Building that pool still reads every eligible post. Sites with a persistent object cache can reuse the pool for 10 minutes. Mullenweg’s view is that searches and REST calls already offer more ways to strain a site. Teams with large archives can watch for repeated hits on /random/ in their logs after the update.

    Agency managers running multiple sites will likely handle /random/ in the same way across their entire fleet using a mu-plugin with the correct spelling of the filter.

    Plugin developers can opt public post types out of /random/ where a random visit makes no sense. They’ll also want to check admin CSS for the icon change and revision any integration that calls the content, user, and settings abilities.

    Industry observers note that mullenweg’s /random/ comment about URL structure could lead to changes to the original /random/ blueprint. Many commenters (on the developer note) are opposed to the default.

    Sources indicate that when the Secrets API returns, and with what design, is now open too. Sites using the AI plugin’s Key Encryption will need to see how its next release handles the revert.

    Whether /random/ will honor SEO plugins’ noindex settings is still an open question. The release date itself has two values on WordPress.org. The release schedule says Dec. 8, while the roadmap still lists Dec. 10.

    It has been revealed that RC1 on Nov. 17 will include the Field Guide and the 7.2 branch. This should help identify where /random/ ended up. RC2 is set to be released Nov. 24, and RC3 Dec. 1. A dry run and code freeze for Dec. 7 precede the scheduled release on Dec. 8. Agent connection work, broader than just connecting an MCP, along with authorization work in core, is targeted for WordPress 7.3.

    To test if /random/ can access your content and how this impacts caching, you’ll need to install RC1 onto a staging version of your website.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    WordPress unveiled the release of version 7.1.5, a security revision that fixes 18 vulnerabilities plus two security improvements. The update addresses several types of vulnerabilities, including cross-site scripting and SQL injection, as well as an unauthenticated flaw that could lead to remote code execution.

    WordPress 7.1.5 fixes 20 issues covering a range of vulnerabilities across WordPress core. One of the vulnerabilities in particular stands out because it could lead to remote code execution (RCE), a type of flaw that can result in a site takeover.

    Sources indicate that the first one that stands out is an unauthenticated privilege escalation vulnerability affecting the Template Part block attributes which could lead to remote code execution (RCE), a type of flaw that can result in a site takeover. There is no authentication required to exploit this vulnerability, and it could lead to RCE. That combination is the worst-case scenario for a CMS.

    According to recent reports, A remote code execution (RCE) is a vulnerability that enables an attacker to run their own code on someone else’s server from somewhere else, usually over the internet. For a WordPress site, that means the attacker can make the web server execute commands of their choosing. From there they can read or change files and make entries to the database, create admin accounts, install backdoors, or inject malware.

    Sources indicate that multisite Administrator to Super Admin takeover (Customizer menu previews). This vulnerability requires an Administrator account, but on a multisite installation that means that an attacker who achieves admin level credential on one site can attain control of the entire network of sites.

    It has been revealed that unauthenticated stored XSS via shortcode attributes in comments. No login is needed to exploit it. Stored XSS is a type of flaw that can run malicious code in the browser of anyone who views the affected comment, including administrators, which can lead to account takeover.

    Two SQL injection vulnerabilities:.

    According to recent reports, wordPress urges site owners to update to version 7.1.5 immediately to address security vulnerabilities. The update is available through the WordPress dashboard or as a download, with automatic updates supported. Security fixes are also available for older affected WordPress versions, although only the latest version is actively supported.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 17, Chrome 158 rolls out to the majority of desktop and mobile owners and drops support for client-side XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations).
    • Industry observers note that for years, WordPress core and major SEO plugins, including Yoast SEO, Rank Math, and All in One SEO (AIOSEO), have referenced an .xsl stylesheet inside their XML sitemaps.
    • Without XSLT support, opening a WordPress sitemap in Chrome 158 displays raw, unstyled XML markup alongside a browser console and page warning.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Nov. 17, Chrome 158 rolls out to the majority of desktop and mobile owners and drops support for client-side XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations).

    Industry observers note that for years, WordPress core and major SEO plugins, including Yoast SEO, Rank Math, and All in One SEO (AIOSEO), have referenced an .xsl stylesheet inside their XML sitemaps. When a person opened a sitemap URL in a browser, Chrome executed that XSLT file to transform the underlying XML code into a clean, clickable HTML table.

    Without XSLT support, opening a WordPress sitemap in Chrome 158 displays raw, unstyled XML markup alongside a browser console and page warning.

    Screenshot from author, November 2026.

    It has been revealed that search engines do not use XSLT. Googlebot, Bingbot, and other web crawlers fetch and parse the raw XML nodes (, ) at the source. Crawlers avoid browser-side stylesheets, meaning indexing, crawl efficiency, and search rankings remain unaffected.

    Because Chrome 158 lands while Google’s November core enhancement, which began on Nov. 10, is still rolling, site owners and clients checking their domains during routine ranking audits may panic when they see raw XML in place of the familiar formatted table.

    Depending on your site configuration, WordPress serves its sitemap index from one of two primary URLs:.

    If you open either URL in Chrome 158 or a newer release, seeing a wall of XML tags confirms the browser skipped the XSLT stylesheet, not that the sitemap file is corrupt or broken.

    Screenshot from author, November 2026.

    To verify, or prove to a nervous client, that Google reads the sitemap without trouble, check Google Search Console:.

    As long as Search Console reports “Success,” Google parses the XML structure without error.

    According to recent reports, XML sitemaps exist for machine consumption, and search engine bots read the underlying and tags. Dropping visual styling changes nothing about URL discovery, crawl budget, or search visibility.

    Because Chrome 158 arrives alongside the November core upgrade, clients or stakeholders who inspect their sitemap URLs will spot unformatted XML code and assume a site outage or plugin failure caused ranking fluctuations.

    It has been revealed that chrome logs a deprecation warning in DevTools whenever a page invokes an .xsl stylesheet. Automated site-health crawlers or QA tools that monitor browser console errors may flag sitemap URLs until plugins or WordPress core drop the stylesheet reference.

    Editors and junior marketers who relied on opening /sitemap_index.xml in Chrome as a quick directory of site URLs lose that visual table unless they switch browsers (such as Firefox or Safari, which retain XSLT for the time being) or use a dedicated HTML sitemap.

    According to recent reports, because search crawlers ignore XSLT, you don’t need to rush to make emergency fixes. Choose from the steps below based on your role and client needs:.

    Note: This is only a visual change. Chrome 158’s removal of XSLT support only affects how sitemaps render in human browsers. Search engine crawlers process raw XML directly and are completely unaffected.

    Organic performance, indexing, and rankings remain safe. WordPress 7.2 will remove the stylesheet reference and, with it, the Chrome warnings, leaving core sitemaps as plain XML. Yoast SEO 28.9 will restore a styled view using CSS, while Rank Math and AIOSEO have not announced a change.

    #20690. Google’s Next Update Won’t Touch The Index, And Nobody Will Announce It via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1728 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Google’s Next Update Won’t Touch The Index, And Nobody Will Announce It via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The viral version of Google’s latest research post says the model makes itself smarter, and the post itself says something more useful to anyone whose job depends on what Google remembers about their company.
    • In March I argued that the training data cutoff had become a ranking factor, because content on the two sides of the cutoff lives in different systems with different confidence behavior, and I suggested timing important claims to land before major training runs.
    • Industry observers note that the post describes a two-phase lifecycle.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The viral version of Google’s latest research post says the model makes itself smarter, and the post itself says something more useful to anyone whose job depends on what Google remembers about their company. On Oct. 27, Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni of Google Research published the sleep framework, a method that gives a language model a scheduled offline phase in which it moves what it picked up during use into its long-term weights, then rehearses on data it generates for itself. The viral framing is wrong in a specific way: the post states that the method operates within a fixed architecture under human-defined training rules, so nothing is modifying itself without supervision. What that framing misses is the part that matters here. If this design ships, the knowledge inside Google’s models stops being frozen at a cutoff and starts updating on a cycle that nobody outside Google will see.

    In March I argued that the training data cutoff had become a ranking factor, because content on the two sides of the cutoff lives in different systems with different confidence behavior, and I suggested timing important claims to land before major training runs. That advice assumed the cutoff was a wall with a date on it. This paper describes a wall that moves on its own schedule, without a date, and the right way to read it is as the next form of the Google upgrade: one that changes what the model believes rather than how the index is ranked, and that arrives with no announcement because there is no event to announce.

    Industry observers note that the post describes a two-phase lifecycle. During a wake phase, the model takes input and holds new information in fast, short-term memory components, which is roughly what context does today. During a sleep phase, it stops taking input and runs two stages. The first is consolidation. The model unlocks new, previously dormant low-rank experts inside a mixture-of-experts layout, assigns them to slower-updating memory blocks, and distills the short-term traces into them through a process the authors call knowledge seeding, which in plain terms means the new facts get their own fresh parameters rather than being written over old ones. Then the temporary parameters are reset so the capacity can be reused. The second stage is what the authors call dreaming. The model generates synthetic samples by randomly routing across its experts so that knowledge from different domains mixes, filters those samples with a gradient-based selection method, and fine-tunes on the ones that survive.

    Industry observers note that the reported results come from four settings: sequential translation into languages the model had never seen, where standard fine-tuning and in-context approaches forgot earlier languages, and the sleep model held a near-zero performance drop; recall on a long-context benchmark out to ten million tokens; factual knowledge incorporation from document passages, where the sleep model beat supervised fine-tuning and a prior self-editing method; and math reasoning on an open 8-billion-parameter base model. The underlying paper has been on arXiv since June and on OpenReview since September 2025, so the blog post is Google deciding to say this out loud, not Google discovering it.

    This is not a one-off. The same authors published Nested Learning in November 2025 with the Hope architecture and the idea of a continuum memory system, a chain of memory blocks that enhancement at different frequencies, with the fast blocks holding short-term information and the slow blocks holding durable knowledge. The sleep framework is what you build once you have blocks that update at different rates: a schedule for moving information from the fast ones to the slow ones. Titans came before Hope, Hope came before sleep, and the arc now runs about two years. The autoregressive ranking paper I covered in September closed a five-year arc on how results get ordered. This one is younger and just as deliberate.

    Industry observers note that it is research, not a product. The post makes no statement about deployment, timelines, or which Google models might use it. The experiments run on open Qwen models at 1.7 and 8 billion parameters, not on Gemini. No compute cost is reported for a sleep cycle, and no one outside the team has replicated the results. In the experiments, the new facts arrive as documents, not as user conversations or crawled web pages, so anyone claiming the model learns from your chats is extrapolating past the paper.

    Those caveats are real and they do not change things. Google publishes research arcs and then ships pieces of them, and that pattern has held often enough that the practitioner question is not whether this exact method lands but what the design tells you about the direction. The direction is a model whose long-term memory is rewritten on a cycle.

    Industry observers note that anyone who has done this work for more than a few years lived through the first version of this shift. Google says it updates Search thousands of times a year and shares only the ones it considers notable, and in a 2022 interview Danny Sullivan put the previous year’s experiments and quality tests above 800,000. The named core updates are the handful that get a dashboard entry. Everything else lands continuously and silently, and the industry adapted by building a diagnostic ritual around the named few: traffic moves, you check the date against the patch trackers, and attribution follows.

    Sources indicate that retrieval already took the same path for freshness. AI Overviews and grounded answers pull latest pages daily with nothing announced, so a claim that silence is new would be wrong. What the sleep framework changes is which layer goes silent. Retrieval changes what the model can look up. Consolidation changes what the model believes without looking anything up. Those are different things for a brand. A retrieved fact is cited, hedged, and replaceable the next time the page is fetched. A consolidated fact is spoken with the confidence of something the model knows, and the March piece covered why that confidence difference shapes how a brand appears in an answer.

    So the shape practitioners already know, confirmed core updates on the outside and unannounced tweaks between them, gets a second copy one layer down: announced model versions on the outside, unannounced consolidation accumulating between them. The ranking stack does not go away and this does not replace it. It sits on top of it, in the model that writes the answer.

    According to recent reports, the detail in the post I keep returning to is that consolidation is selective. The authors say the model is not asked to copy every detail from its short-term traces into its parameters, and the dreaming stage scores its own samples with a gradient-based filter before anything is trained on. That is a ranking function. It decides which facts the model will carry forward as durable knowledge and which it will let expire with the temporary parameters. Being seen during wake is not being learned. Being learned is what being indexed used to mean, and the thing deciding it is a loss calculation nobody outside Google can inspect.

    Three consequences follow, and the first two are my inference from the design rather than claims the paper makes.

    First, the filter will favor facts that are consistent across sources. A gradient-based selection method keeps samples that reduce error broadly, and a fact that agrees with everything else the model has seen reduces error more reliably than one that contradicts a competitor’s page, a stale directory listing, or your own older content. Conflicting versions of your manufacturer are no longer only a conflation risk at retrieval time, which I covered when German courts started holding the platform responsible for false answers, but a consolidation risk, because the version that gets learned is the one that fits best, not the one you prefer.

    Industry observers note that second, dreaming means the model rehearses on data you never published. The synthetic samples are generated by mixing experts across domains, so the model’s representation of a firm can shift through rehearsal with no new input from anyone. No competitor moved, no page changed, no update ran, and the answer about you is different anyway. This is a candidate mechanism for a question I have been asked repeatedly this year, which is why an answer changed when nothing observable changed.

    Third, and this one sits in the paper’s design directly, there is a window. Between a fact entering the fast memory and the next consolidation, a correction is cheap because nothing durable has been written yet. After consolidation, fixing a false fact is no longer a matter of updating a page and waiting for a recrawl. It is unlearning, and removing one specific fact from a model’s weights without damaging the rest remains an open research problem. The term I would use is the consolidation window, the period in which a wrong fact can still be caught before the model commits it, and the uncomfortable property of the window is that its length and timing are unknown to you.

    If no Google model announcement within roughly 18 months references periodic updates between releases, continual learning in production, or anything resembling a consolidation cycle, this stays a research direction, and the cutoff stays a wall. If the compute cost of a sleep cycle turns out to be comparable to a training run, the economics kill the cadence idea even if the method works. And if Google chooses to publish consolidation events the way it publishes core updates, the silence argument fails and the diagnostic ritual survives with a upcoming row on the dashboard. I think the third is the least likely of the three, because Google has never published its unnamed changes and has noted plainly that it does not intend to.

    The useful response is to stop building process around an event that may stop existing.

    The cutoff-aware calendaring I suggested in March still holds for the next major training run, because those will keep happening. What changes is the half-life of the word parametric. The safest assumption is that what the model knows about you is being revised on a schedule you cannot see, by a filter you cannot inspect, and that the only observable is the answer itself.

    This post was originally published on Duane Forrester Decodes.

    21 Alternative Search Engines You Can Use Instead of Google via @sejournal, @lorenbaker

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that for many people, searching the web means opening Google.
    • But the search engine you use out of habit is not always the best tool for the job.
    • That is where alternatives earn their place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that for many people, searching the web means opening Google. It’s a familiar place to research a purchase, check a fact, or catch up on the news and that reach highlights in the numbers with Google accounting for 91.04% of worldwide search engine referrals according to Statcounter in October 2026.

    But the search engine you use out of habit is not always the best tool for the job. Think about the last time you needed an image you could reuse, a webpage that had disappeared, or a more private way to search. Those are different problems, and a single search box is not always the easiest way to solve them.

    That is where alternatives earn their place. Some give you more control over privacy and rankings, whilst others bring together sources in a conversation, search a specialist collection, or help you explore the content people use in another country. For marketers, those differences also explain why visibility beyond Google involves more than submitting a website to another engine.

    Sources indicate that you don’t have to give up Google to find out what you might be missing. We collated 21 alternative search engines and tools worth trying, whether you’re looking for a better answer or a upcoming way for customers to find your business.

    In a recent development, about the Usage Figures: Entries are ordered within each section by estimated monthly visits to the named website or subdomain. The October 2026 figures are not unique people, search queries, or app activity. Statcounter percentages shown separately measure search referral share, not visits.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 6 billion to chatgpt.com, October 2026. This covers the ChatGPT website, not Search alone.

    Recent findings suggest that chatGPT is useful when your question needs a conversation rather than a fresh set of keywords each time. You can ask it to compare two approaches, explain an unfamiliar term, and then look for recent evidence without starting over. Its advantage is keeping the context of that investigation together.

    OpenAI’s search documentation notes it can retrieve current web information and link to sources. Search is available on free and paid plans, including for people who are not signed in, although usage limits apply. ChatGPT may search automatically, or you can select Search from its tools.

    In a recent development, use it to work through a question, then open the citations to check the answer. It can misread a source or miss a qualification, and its use of other search providers means it is not simply a separate, independent web index.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 88.3 million to perplexity.ai, October 2026.

    Sources indicate that perplexity puts source-backed answers at the center of the search experience. Its research-oriented approach is useful when you want an overview of a subject and a trail of sources to investigate, rather than opening a long list of results before finding the main points.

    In a recent development, its Pro Search process can conduct multiple searches and bring findings together, with follow-up questions keeping the research in context. Depending on your blueprint, you can narrow the work to areas such as academic or financial sources. Access and limits vary by tier.

    The benefit is a faster route into a topic, not a substitute for reading the evidence. Check that each citation supports the statement beside it because AI answers can still contain hallucinations even when links are present.

    Sources indicate that why SEO Experts Should Care: Perplexity can be useful even if it sends less traffic than Google. In his post on why marketers should care about Perplexity, Dennis Goedegebuure argues that it is a low-cost test bench for AI search. Try the research questions your customers ask, inspect which pages get cited, and check how your brand and recently updated facts appear. For B2B marketers, that means testing visibility during product research, rather than judging the opportunity solely by overall visit totals.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 3.7 billion to bing.com, October 2026.

    Industry observers note that bing is a full-service alternative for everyday web, image, video, and news searches. One concrete reason to try it is Visual Search: when you have a picture of a product, plant, or object but do not know its name, you can start with the image instead of guessing keywords.

    Microsoft’s visual search tools can find related images and shopping options, identify objects, and extract or translate text from a picture. Conventional results remain available alongside AI-assisted tools, so an answer does not have to be the end of your search.

    Search Engine Journal covered Bing’s search updates in December 2024, including work on faster, more precise results. Try the same image or video query on Bing and Google to see which makes the next step easier for you; that is more useful than assuming one wins every search.

    Where available, Bing’s Copilot Search adds AI-generated summaries with source citations and suggested follow-up topics, so you can explore a question without starting from scratch.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 751 million to search.yahoo.com, October 2026.

    Search Engine Referral Share: 2.54% in the U.S., October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Yahoo Search makes the most sense if you already use Yahoo for news, finance, or other daily information. Its value is the connection between search and that wider content ecosystem, rather than a completely different index of the web.

    Recent findings suggest that yahoo introduced Scout in January 2026 as an AI answer engine combining open-web information with Yahoo content and data. The U.S. beta launch named Anthropic’s Claude and Microsoft’s Bing grounding API as parts of the system.

    Recent findings suggest that that gives Yahoo users a way to move from a headline or financial topic into a sourced explanation. You can still browse traditional search results, and you should follow Scout’s source links when an answer matters. The launch’s audience figures cover Yahoo’s broader services, not people using Scout alone.

    At Search Engine Journal, Yahoo accounts for about 0.2% of our traffic. It’s a small share, but it still brings a few thousand visits in a month and for a different business, even that smaller stream of visitors could include a potential customer or lead to a sale.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 1.7 billion to baidu.com, October 2026. This includes non-search activity on the named website.

    According to recent reports, search Engine Referral Share: 49% in China, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Baidu matters when your research or marketing is aimed at Chinese-language audiences. Its value is not simply in translating an English query, but it offers a view of Chinese-language search and a connected set of local content services.

    According to recent reports, alongside web results, its homepage links to maps, images, video, the Baike encyclopedia, Zhidao questions and answers, and Wenku documents. Those services give you distinct places to investigate how a topic, product, or brand is described. Use the terminology that local sources use rather than assuming an English search will surface the same material.

    Sources indicate that for marketers, the search referral share is a reason to investigate Baidu separately, not proof that it will send a particular site traffic. Distinguish content hosted inside Baidu’s services from results linking to external publishers, and assess the original source.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 1.5 billion to naver.com, October 2026. This includes non-search activity on the named website.

    Search Engine Referral Share: 42.25% in South Korea, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    Sources indicate that naver is useful for Korean-language research because its search experience brings together more than external webpages. Naver’s search overview describes results across news, maps, cafés, blogs, images, video, and other categories.

    In a recent development, that mix gives you a route into local experiences and community content as well as conventional reporting. Its community services include Naver Blog, interest-based Café communities, and Knowledge iN questions and answers. If you are researching a Korean product or audience, those are different sources to explore from an English-language web-results page.

    For website owners, Naver Search Advisor is the official starting point for webmaster tools. Keep visits to an external website separate from engagement with a blog or other content hosted inside Naver.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 162.2 million to yandex.com, October 2026. This covers the international website, not total use across all Yandex domains.

    Search Engine Referral Share: 70.22% in Russia, October 2026. This measures referrals in its sample, not people or total queries.

    In a recent development, yandex is worth checking when you need Russian-language sources or are researching visibility in Russia. Its large share of measured referrals there gives it a different role from a small global alternative – it is an vital regional search environment in its own right.

    Use it to compare which local publishers and pages appear for the terminology your audience actually uses. Its international homepage also presents an AI search option, but the practical reason to investigate it is the regional results and audience context, not simply another chatbot interface.

    SEJ’s Yandex guide provides background for marketers. The 2023 data leak is a separate historical event, not a verified description of today’s ranking system. The search referral share above describes referrals, not the percentage of Russian people using Yandex.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 16.5 million to sogou.com, October 2026.

    Sogou offers another route into Chinese-language information, with a more specific reason to try it rather than simply comparing general web results – its WeChat search is a destination for discovering public accounts and articles from that ecosystem.

    That is useful when the material you need was published as a WeChat article rather than an ordinary standalone webpage. Search in the relevant Chinese terminology and distinguish those public articles from results in Sogou’s general web search.

    Recent findings suggest that this is not access to private messages or every piece of content in WeChat. As with other platform-specific searches, check the account, publication date, and original article before using a result as evidence.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 698.8 million to search.brave.com, October 2026.

    Brave Search combines an independent web index with tools for changing how results are ranked. It is worth trying if you want both an alternative to Google or Bing’s underlying results and more say over which sources rise to the top.

    Its search help describes Goggles, which apply alternative ranking or filtering rules. Brave also describes domain-level ranking controls and an AI answer experience on its about page. Those controls give you something more specific to experiment with than a different-looking results page.

    SEJ reported Brave’s Bing separation in 2023. You can use Brave Search in another browser, so testing its index does not require adopting Brave’s browser, wallet, VPN, or other products.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 681.9 million to duckduckgo.com, October 2026.

    DuckDuckGo is a straightforward choice if you want everyday search without a personal search-history profile. You can use its search website in your existing browser, so the switch does not require changing your whole browsing setup.

    Privacy and index independence are different benefits, however. DuckDuckGo’s source documentation indicates traditional links and images largely come from Bing, supplemented by specialist sources, its own crawler, and its own indexes. Choose it for that privacy model, not on the assumption that every result comes from a separate web index.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 57.6 million to startpage.com, October 2026.

    It has been revealed that startpage is for people who want results from major search providers without dealing with those providers directly. It acts as a privacy intermediary, submitting your query on your behalf and returning the results to you.

    Its partner explanation identifies both Google and Microsoft Bing. Startpage says it does not share personal information with them, and that those providers see Startpage rather than the person making the request.

    According to recent reports, that is the distinction from an independent-index engine: Startpage changes the relationship between you and the search provider, not necessarily the underlying collection of pages. It is worth trying if you like familiar results but want a different privacy arrangement; it is not a way to avoid Google’s infrastructure altogether.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 4.6 million to kagi.com, October 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that its Lenses let you narrow searches to selected websites or categories such as forums, academic sources, or PDFs. Kagi’s source documentation describes its own indexes alongside major and specialist providers, with an emphasis on surfacing independent and noncommercial content. It is not powered solely by its Teclis index.

    Industry observers note that as of November 2026, its monthly individual intends include Starter at $5 plus tax for 300 searches and Professional at $10 plus tax for unlimited searches. Annual billing has different terms. If you search heavily and want persistent control over sources, those features are the reason to consider paying.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 219 million to ecosia.org, October 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that ecosia lets you put the revenue from an everyday habit toward climate work. It notes all of its profits go to climate action, with the majority funding tree-planting projects. That is its central reason to exist: changing who benefits financially from search.

    The tech giant publishes monthly financial reports, so you can look beyond the tree counter to see how money is spent. Its provider documentation lists Bing, Google, and European Search Perspective, or EUSP; the mix depends on factors including region, device, and permissions.

    Recent findings suggest that this makes Ecosia a funding-model choice, not a promise that every query uses a wholly separate index. If you want to support its mission while keeping familiar web search, it is a low-friction option to try. You can check the provider through the information control beside a result.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 451,800 to karmasearch.org, October 2026.

    KARMA applies the search-funded nonprofit model to animal welfare and biodiversity. Its distinction from a broader climate-focused service is the cause: helping fund organizations working on wildlife, habitats, and animal protection.

    The manufacturer’s explanation states sponsored search links generate revenue for its nonprofit partners. Its site lists partners including Re:wild, Humane World for Animals, and iNaturalist. You can inspect those partnerships to decide whether they match the work you want to support.

    Availability varies by country. During this review, a U.S. capture highlighted the search homepage, while a visit from another region displayed a notice that KARMA was unavailable there and would redirect searches to Bing. Check local availability before making it your default; a regional restriction does not mean the service has closed.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 155,800 to yep.com, October 2026.

    Yep is an Ahrefs-built alternative with a distinctive audience beyond people typing into a search box: developers who want web results for an AI agent or research application. Ahrefs’ current Yep product page describes a first-party crawler, index, and ranking system, with result excerpts and filters for the information an application retrieves.

    Industry observers note that the public search interface captured for this review also returned conventional web results. For an everyday user, that makes it another index to compare; for a developer, the API is the clearer reason to investigate it. The current homepage emphasizes that developer-facing use rather than presenting a Google-like consumer pitch.

    Industry observers note that SEJ’s 2022 Yep interview explains the original proposal to share advertising revenue with creators. Although, the current homepage does not establish that those proposed payouts are operating, so they should not be the reason you choose it today.

    Sources indicate that estimated Monthly Web Visits: 4.4 billion to x.com, October 2026. This covers platform website activity, not searches or app usage.

    x.com is useful when the thing you need is a public statement or conversation: what an organization announced, what a named person mentioned, or how a developing event is being discussed. You are searching posts on the platform, not a general index of webpages.

    That direct access to posted statements is its advantage for news monitoring and research. Its advanced search is a further option for signed-in consumers; the public Explore route redirected to a sign-in screen during this review.

    Sources indicate that use posts to locate leads and original statements, not as automatic confirmation of a claim. Check the account, timestamp, and supporting evidence, especially when an old post is circulating as if it describes a new event.

    Recent findings suggest that estimated Monthly Web Visits: 2.1 billion to linkedin.com, October 2026. This covers platform website activity, not searches or app usage.

    Recent findings suggest that linkedIn is useful when your search starts with a professional identity, such as a person, employer, role, or job. It can also help you find practitioners discussing a work-related subject, rather than only the publishers ranking for that subject on the open web.

    The advantage is the professional context. A name alongside an employer and career history gives you a way to distinguish people who share a name and identify a relevant source. Its public people search is one starting point, although fuller profiles and other features can require signing in.

    It has been revealed that treat profiles as self-reported information, not a verified company directory. Check current roles and dates against the person’s or organization’s own website when those details matter to your research.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 46.4 million to web.archive.org, October 2026.

    Industry observers note that the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine answers a question a current search result often cannot: What did this webpage say before it changed or disappeared? It is useful for checking an old product claim, recovering a removed reference, or following the history of a website.

    It has been revealed that enter the URL and inspect the available captures. The advantage is the dated record where you can compare versions rather than relying on a current page to explain its own past. Check the capture date and whether images and other resources were preserved.

    Industry observers note that the Wayback Machine is part of the wider Internet Archive, whose books, recordings, software, and other collections are separate resources. It is not a complete archive of every page, and a captured claim is evidence of what a page stated then, not proof that the claim was true.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 39.3 million to slideshare.net, October 2026.

    SlideShare is worth trying when you want the presentation itself, not another article summarizing the subject. A conference talk, research deck, or business pitch can reveal how someone structures an argument and illustrates the details.

    The current homepage describes a collection of more than 25 million presentations. Browsing, reading, and uploading do not require a subscription, while features such as downloading presentations are paid benefits. The value is a format-specific collection you can explore for research or presentation inspiration.

    Recent findings suggest that check the uploader and publication date before relying on a deck’s statistics or recommendations. Being able to view a presentation also does not automatically give you permission to reuse its artwork.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 3.1 million to wolframalpha.com, October 2026.

    In a recent development, wolframAlpha is for questions that need computation rather than a list of pages. If you want to solve an equation, convert units, or work with structured facts, it can calculate an answer from its data and algorithms instead of leaving you to find a suitable calculator elsewhere.

    In a recent development, its explanation of the service describes dynamic computation over curated knowledge. The mathematics examples show the inputs it understands; other areas include science, dates, and measures.

    In a recent development, that is a different job from comparing recent reporting or finding an opinion. Use it when the result should be computed, and check how it interpreted your units, assumptions, and wording before relying on the output.

    Estimated Monthly Web Visits: 296,200 to openverse.org, October 2026.

    Openverse is the tool to try when finding a usable image or audio track matters more than finding a webpage about one. It focuses on openly licensed and public-domain media, making it useful for an article, presentation, or other creative project.

    Its About page describes a collection of more than 800 million images and audio tracks gathered from multiple repositories, with features such as one-click attribution. That collection size is separate from its website traffic. Its advantage is bringing reuse-oriented discovery into one place, rather than treating every image on the web as equally available to use.

    Openly licensed does not mean free of conditions. Licenses can require attribution or restrict commercial use, and Openverse does not verify every work’s licensing information. Follow through to the original source and confirm the license before using a file.

    The introduction of ChatGPT helped bring conversational interfaces into everyday use. In January 2023, SEJ reported that Google’s founders had responded by returning to discussions about its AI response and then opened access to Bard in March 2023.

    Google rolled out AI Overviews to U.S. users in May 2024 and declared AI Mode in 2025. Those developments explain why many services in this list now combine web results with AI generated answers. The two formats can help with different parts of the same research task.

    Google may be the most familiar option, but the best choice for a particular task can be different. Try a few real queries on two or three services, compare the sources, the ease of finding the original information, and the controls you will actually use.

    In a recent development, you can keep one engine for everyday searches and use another for a specific job. A calculation, an archived webpage, and a professional profile do not need to start in the same search box.

    Featured Image: Igor Link/Shutterstock.

    Open your browser’s search settings and choose a supported default engine. If the service is not listed, use its official browser setup instructions. You can also visit its website directly without changing your default.

    Start with the task you want to improve. Try Bing for general web search, DuckDuckGo for a search service centered on privacy, Brave Search for another independent index, and ChatGPT or Perplexity for conversational answers. Compare their results on queries you already know well.

    It has been revealed that some do. Startpage identifies Google and Bing as partners. DuckDuckGo largely sources traditional links and images from Bing. Kagi combines its own indexes with several providers. Brave Search builds an independent web index.

    No. DuckDuckGo notes it is an independent manufacturer. A search provider relationship is different from ownership, and its traditional links and images largely come from Bing.

    No search tool can guarantee a neutral view of everything online. Index coverage, ranking rules, filters, location, and the query itself affect what appears. Compare independent sources and more than one search engine when the differences matter.

    It has been revealed that business models vary. Some display search advertising, some charge subscriptions, and some combine free and paid services. Read the specific service’s policy because a privacy claim does not mean every product, advertisement, and linked website handles data in the same way.

    AI Citations: What To Check Before Reacting To A Lost One via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Around three in four AI citation drops were temporary, according to Ahrefs’ study of the changes in five different AI products over 20 days.
    • Recent findings suggest that when sharing AI citation analysis results with clients or bosses, you should be aware that a loss may not represent what it seems like at first glance.
    • In a recent development, ahrefs studied about 37,500 first-day citations made by Google’s AI Mode and AI Overviews, along with ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Around three in four AI citation drops were temporary, according to Ahrefs’ study of the changes in five different AI products over 20 days.

    Recent findings suggest that when sharing AI citation analysis results with clients or bosses, you should be aware that a loss may not represent what it seems like at first glance. Sites in the study that had been cited in answers but then dropped out of those answers were more likely to have another citation occur for them as opposed to staying missing. If someone rewrote a page in the meantime, that rewrite could receive credit for a citation it didn’t earn.

    In a recent development, ahrefs studied about 37,500 first-day citations made by Google’s AI Mode and AI Overviews, along with ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot. The study included only one organization’s view based on its own group of questions answered daily by each tool for 20 days.

    The study’s findings point to four items to look into before making an edit to a webpage based upon the disappearance of a citation.

    Tracking the same citations for consecutive days, the study was able to see what can happen after a site has disappeared from an answer.

    In a recent development, these results were documented by Mateusz Makosiewicz, an SEO and marketing educator at Ahrefs. His colleague Xibeijia Guan collected all websites that had been cited on day one, then traced each reference through to day 20.

    According to recent reports, by day two, about half of those references were gone from AI Overviews. Even more were gone on each of the other tools. Most of these returned prior to the conclusion of the study.

    Across the five tools, about half of the citations that dropped out came back within three days, Ahrefs found.

    The data collected in this study reflects the number of websites, thus when a website comes back, this study cannot determine whether the exact same webpage came back as well.

    In a recent development, another measure was taken (in Brand Radar’s own tracking of citations), revealing a somewhat comparable pattern with lower rates of return. About two-thirds of all the citations that disappeared from view there ultimately did come back. Ahrefs sells Brand Radar, and the write-up has a section on using it.

    Earlier research I have discussed demonstrated changes in AI responses over multiple runs of a prompt, and this current study adds what happens across different days.

    I reported on SparkToro’s findings in January regarding their discovery that both ChatGPT and Google’s AI in Search provided the same list of brands less than 1% of the time across repeated runs of the same prompt. They also found that the frequency with which a brand appeared throughout multiple runs was generally more stable than the specific ranking of that brand within those lists.

    The fresh study’s authors recommend counting how many of the last seven days a site was cited. This is a frequency count by day for the sites that were cited and the research in January favored a frequency count by run for brand names.

    When a loss occurred on Gemini or Copilot, it often meant there was no one cited at all in the response.

    Recent findings suggest that gemini had responses without citations about 64% of the time in the data from this study, while Copilot showed answers without citations around 53% of the time. Without citations in an answer, a site will appear as a loss when you track your results.

    It has been revealed that many of the comebacks on those two tools were the tool citing sources again after an answer that cited none. With the empty answers left out, Gemini and Copilot looked much like AI Mode and ChatGPT.

    Recent findings suggest that AI Overviews, AI Mode and ChatGPT almost always cited sources. Fewer than 1% of their answers had no citations, and Makosiewicz wrote that a lost citation on those tools almost always means another site took the spot.

    Recent findings suggest that the first way to verify a lost citation is by looking at the answer. If the answer has no link then you are getting information about the AI tool that day, while if the answer links to a competitor then you have found the site that was cited in your place.

    On Gemini and Copilot, per the write-up, you should keep track of two metrics, the number of times your site gets cited, as well as the frequency with which references are made to another source instead.

    Citations that had stayed active longer before going away were more likely to come back.

    The study ranked all citations on three of the tools (AI Overviews, AI Mode and ChatGPT) in order of how long they had been there until they went away the first time.

    For those with a short life span (one day), 34% to 41% of the citations did not return during the study period.

    And for those that remained there for eight to 14 days, this percentage was at or below 4%.

    This suggests that a citation’s history may be more important than where it stands on a given day. A site referenced once that then disappears is an entirely different circumstance than a site that has maintained its position for 10 days and disappeared yesterday.

    An analysis of occasional check-in reports indicates if a site was cited on a specific date (so every site with only one appearance looks like every other site with continuous appearances). Using a seven-day count allows a team to make a distinction. It counts, for each question being asked, the number of days out of the last seven the site was a source referenced. This shows how often a site turns up. How long one citation held is a separate question.

    This process also provides a team with an ongoing assessment of whether an AI tool is consistently relying on a given site to answer those questions.

    In a recent development, similarly, it can be applied to newly introduced citations. In terms of evaluating the usefulness of a new citation as a lasting win, Makosiewicz suggests waiting a few days before declaring victory. His general rule is to view one missing citation as no reason to change a page, but to review the page if the citation is still missing after two or three weeks.

    A brand can still be named in an answer even after the link to its site disappears.

    Sources indicate that A citation is a link readers can follow. A mention is a brand name in the answer text, whether or not it includes a link.

    Each tool used saw approximately 50% to 70% of all cited sites appear on only one day, as opposed to around one in five of all brands named.

    In a recent development, then your report can display a lost citation while the answer still names the organization. The link is still absent, and it still counts as a lost citation, and looking at the answer will tell you which measure has changed.

    Recent findings suggest that also, AI tools use different versions (longer or shorter) of the same brand name from answer to answer. And a mention that seems to be gone could be the same organization referred to by a different name, so the write-up advises checking for this before subtracting it from your mention totals.

    Since the data indicated brand names were not moving nearly as much as citations, Makosiewicz suggests that mentions may be the better metric to follow.

    On AI Overviews and AI Mode, pages that also ranked in Google Search for the same question kept their citations longer.

    In this portion of the study, the authors examined pages. They compared cited pages that appeared somewhere within Google’s results for a question versus those that did not appear anywhere in Google’s results for the same question. On AI Overviews and AI Mode, cited pages that ranked had greater longevity of citation, more often lasting a week or longer; however, the difference between them was smaller for ChatGPT.

    In a recent development, although appearing in Google’s search results at all correlated with longer-lasting citations more than a page’s exact position in the results list did, according to the write-up, this finding was based on an examination of 230 questions. That comparison highlighted a correlation between whether pages rank in Google searches for each question and how long the citations to these pages last. Ranking wasn’t a requirement, though. Most of the pages AI Mode and ChatGPT cited didn’t rank in Google for the question they were cited on.

    When a citation stays missing, the authors suggest examining two items, how the page performs in Google Search for the question and how well the page answers the question.

    In September, I proposed a related item to be examined when citations drop while rankings hold steady. That item is to examine the pages being cited in lieu of those originally cited.

    Sources indicate that the methodology of this examination also relates to the work performed by SEO teams. When a page loses its Google ranking for a particular question and subsequently drops off of the AI Overview citations, looking into why the page lost its ranking would be a logical starting point to investigate.

    Most citations that disappeared came back during the study, so one comeback alone may not be strong evidence that a page change caused it.

    A team that edits a page after losing a citation and then sees the citation come back has two explanations for it. An edit can’t be credited as working (it may have been due to some other reason) when there is only one comeback to support this.

    Makosiewicz wrote, “Don’t credit a page edit for a single comeback.”.

    In essence, he wants us to look at an increase in the number of times a site reference appears over a longer time span.

    In addition, it would be weak evidence that an edit damaged a citation when that citation disappears the very next day after you edit a page, because half or more of citations disappeared by the next day in the study.

    In a recent development, A number of things can be checked by someone before they change the page behind a lost citation. First, they can look again over the next several days to see whether the citation is still missing. Second, they can read the response itself.

    Management will learn a lot more from a count like five of the last seven, when an in-house team reports how many days a site was cited, than from simply receiving a yes or no from one check.

    An agency has an order to follow on a client call, checking the text of the response, the history of the citation and the ranking of the page prior to making a proposal for new content.

    A content team will get a warning about correlation vs. causation. One comeback after an edit does not provide you with sufficient evidence to make similar edits to other pages.

    The researchers measured the disappearance of citations; they did not test if changing a page brings back a citation that has gone missing.

    It has been revealed that they only tracked the very first time a citation went missing. The data collected does not reveal how frequently those same citations disappeared again after returning.

    The researchers wrote that their figures may represent an underestimate of citations returning as citations that disappeared at the end of the study had less time to return than citations that were lost early in the study. Changes to models could also affect the stability of citation patterns over time.

    According to recent reports, the next lost citation will be much easier to read when you have something to reference already. Having a daily log of which sites are cited, related to the questions that matter most, can help provide your team’s own internal tally of days cited prior to a client or manager asking why citations are down.

    When a citation is still missing after two or three weeks, the study’s advice is to look at the page, beginning with how it ranks for the question.
